newsitem.title: USA: IMF TELLS JAPAN TO KEEP LID ON SHORT-TERM RATES.
newsitem.headline: IMF TELLS JAPAN TO KEEP LID ON SHORT-TERM RATES.

text.p: The strong yen is justified by Japan's robust fundamentals, and Tokyo should keep a lid on short-term interest rates to give its economic revival a chance, the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday.
"Directors believed that the current level of the yen was broadly in line with fundamentals," the IMF's Executive Board said in its annual review of the Japanese economy.

"Directors believed that the current easy stance of monetary policy should be maintained for the time being, but that it would likely be desirable to begin tightening later in the year," the report said.

The IMF, whose comments were released after the United States criticized Japan for not opening markets up quickly enough, said there was a risk that trading partners could retaliate if Japan's current account surplus rose and looked set to stay high.

Japanese short-term rates have been at historic lows for almost two years, helping the country to emerge from a spell of weak growth in 1995. GDP growth accelerated to 3.5 percent last year, one of highest rates in the industrial world, compared with just 1.5 percent in 1995.

The IMF said Japan's economic revival now appeared to be self-sustaining, but it urged the government to maintain its tight grip on spending and continue unwinding the fiscal stimulus package originally aimed at aiding the recovery.
"The central challenge for policymakers (is) to return the fiscal balance to a more sustainable balance over the medium term," the report said.
"Directors endorsed the fiscal correction measures enacted in the 1997 budget deficit as a step in the right direction."

The government earlier this year raised the consumption tax rate, withdrew a range of temporary tax cuts and pledged a range of spending cuts for the 1998 fiscal year in a bid to reduce its huge budget deficit.
Government reports say the Japanese economy is recovering gradually, even though the tax increases caused a temporary slowdown in April.
The IMF said it saw no reason to worry about Japan's present current account surplus, but it foresaw possible retaliation by Japan's trading partners if the surplus began a sustained rise.
U.S. officials have consistently urged Japan to ensure its recovery is led by domestic demand and not let its current account surplus surge past 2.5 percent of gross domestic product.

The fund urged Japan to keep up the pace of deregulation and structural reform to ensure robust growth in the long term. It said one of the key issues for the government to deal with was the health of the country's banking sector.
"Directors welcomed the progress made over the past year in addressing financial sector problems, but noted that the strengthening of the banking system should remain a top priority," it said.
